title: Python Execution & Memory Internals
description: Explore CPython reference counting, generational cyclic GC, the GIL, descriptors, and scoping gotchas.

questions.text: What happens in CPython when two objects reference each other cyclically (e.g., A.child = B and B.parent = A) and all external references to them are deleted?

options.text: They are immediately reclaimed by reference counting because their scope ended
Their reference counts remain at 1, so they survive until the cyclic garbage collector runs and detects the isolated cycle
CPython crashes with a RecursionError during teardown
The operating system forcibly frees the memory pages when the thread context switches

questions.explanation: Reference counting alone cannot free cyclic references because each object retains a non-zero reference count from the other. CPython relies on its secondary cyclic garbage collector, which periodically scans generations of container objects, simulates trial reference decrements, and frees unreachable cyclic subgraphs.

questions.text: In Python's descriptor protocol, what is the crucial behavioral difference between a Data Descriptor and a Non-Data Descriptor?

options.text: Data descriptors can only store strings, while non-data descriptors store functions
A data descriptor defines __set__ or __delete__ and takes precedence over an instance's __dict__; a non-data descriptor only defines __get__ and is shadowed by an instance's __dict__
Non-data descriptors run in C extensions while data descriptors run in pure Python
Data descriptors cannot be used with the @property decorator

questions.explanation: If an object implements __set__ (or __delete__), it is a data descriptor. When an attribute is looked up on an instance (obj.attr), CPython checks the class's data descriptors *before* looking in obj.__dict__. If the class only defines a non-data descriptor (defining only __get__, like regular methods), obj.__dict__ takes precedence and shadows it.

questions.text: Consider the code: `funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]`. What does `[f() for f in funcs]` return, and why?

options.text: [0, 1, 2], because each lambda captures the value of i at the moment it was created
[2, 2, 2], because closures bind names by reference late, looking up the value of i at invocation time when the loop has finished
TypeError, because lambdas cannot access loop variables
[0, 0, 0], because the loop scope resets upon completion

questions.explanation: Python closures bind variables by name late, not by value at definition time. All three lambda functions look up the variable `i` in their enclosing scope when called; by that time, the for-loop has completed and `i` equals 2. To capture current values, use default argument binding: `lambda i=i: i`.

questions.text: What performance and architectural benefits are achieved by defining `__slots__ = ('name', 'age')` on a Python class?

options.text: It eliminates the default `__dict__` attribute dictionary, drastically reducing per-instance memory overhead
It speeds up attribute access by using fixed descriptor offsets instead of hash table lookups
It prevents arbitrary creation of new undeclared attributes on instances
It automatically disables the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) for instances of that class

questions.explanation: Defining `__slots__` tells CPython to allocate a fixed-size C array of pointers for the declared attributes instead of creating an internal `__dict__` hash table for each instance. This reduces memory usage by 60-70%, speeds up attribute access, and prevents callers from assigning arbitrary attributes outside the declared slots.

questions.text: Why does calling `def append_to(item, target=[])` create unexpected state bugs across multiple invocations?

options.text: Default arguments are evaluated once at module load time when the function definition is executed, creating a single shared list
Python garbage collects default lists after the first return
Lists are immutable in function headers
The GIL locks default arguments to prevent thread concurrency

questions.explanation: In Python, default arguments are evaluated once when the function definition is executed (at compile/import time), not each time the function is called. If a mutable object (like a list or dict) is used as a default, every call that relies on the default modifies the exact same underlying object. The idiomatic fix is `def append_to(item, target=None): if target is None: target = []`.

questions.text: In Python asyncio, running a CPU-bound computation like `time.sleep(5)` inside an async function will freeze the entire event loop, stopping all other concurrent tasks.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Asyncio runs a single-threaded cooperative event loop. If a task executes synchronous blocking code (like time.sleep or heavy CPU math) instead of awaiting an asynchronous non-blocking future (`await asyncio.sleep(5)`), the main thread cannot yield control back to the event loop, freezing all concurrent coroutines.

questions.text: What is the primary role of `__new__` versus `__init__` in Python?

options.text: `__new__` initializes attributes; `__init__` compiles the bytecode
`__new__` is the static method that allocates and returns the instance object; `__init__` initializes the newly created instance
`__new__` is called only when an object is deserialized with pickle
They are interchangeable aliases

questions.explanation: `__new__` is the constructor that creates and returns a new object instance (receiving `cls`). `__init__` is the initializer called immediately after `__new__` returns an instance of that class (receiving `self`). Overriding `__new__` is necessary when subclassing immutable types (like tuple or int) or implementing singletons.

questions.text: How does `__exit__` in a context manager suppress an exception raised within the `with` block?

options.text: By setting exc_type to None
By returning a truthy value (such as True)
By executing a break statement
Context managers cannot suppress exceptions

questions.explanation: When an exception occurs inside a `with` statement, the exception's type, value, and traceback are passed into `__exit__(exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)`. If `__exit__` returns a truthy value (e.g. `return True`), CPython suppresses the exception and resumes normal execution immediately after the `with` block.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks (denoted by dashes `___`): 'In CPython, memory management uses immediate reference counting, but cyclic references survive until the _____ collector runs across three _____, while attribute lookup checks the class's _____ descriptors before inspecting the instance `__dict__`.' Which of the following statements are correct?

options.text: The cyclic garbage collector runs across three generations (0, 1, 2) to detect and reclaim unreachable reference cycles
Data descriptors (defining __set__ or __delete__) take precedence over an instance's __dict__
Non-data descriptors (defining only __get__) take precedence over data descriptors
Generational collection is triggered when allocation counts exceed deallocation thresholds

questions.explanation: Cyclic GC reclaims unreferenced cycles across three generations. Data descriptors take precedence over `__dict__`, whereas non-data descriptors are shadowed by `__dict__`.

questions.text:
Examine the architectural box-joining diagram mapping Python execution layers (Boxes 1-4) with dashes `-- (dash) -->` to their runtime artifacts:
[Box 1: Tokenizer / Lexer]   -- (1) --> [Artifact A: Stream of lexical tokens from source code]
[Box 2: PEG Parser]          -- (2) --> [Artifact B: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)]
[Box 3: Bytecode Compiler]   -- (3) --> [Artifact C: PyCodeObject containing bytecode & co_consts]
[Box 4: CPython Eval Loop]   -- (4) --> [Artifact D: ceval.c virtual machine stack evaluation]
Which box-joining pairings accurately trace Python compilation?

options.text: Box 1 -- (1) --> Artifact A is correct (lexical analysis generates tokens)
Box 2 -- (2) --> Artifact B is correct (parser constructs the AST)
Box 3 -- (3) --> Artifact C is correct (compiler emits code objects with bytecode)
Box 4 -- (4) --> Artifact D is correct (ceval.c executes the virtual machine evaluation loop)
Box 1 -- (1) --> Artifact C is correct (tokenizer directly generates code objects)

questions.explanation: Stages 1 to 4 accurately trace the CPython pipeline from source tokens to AST, bytecode compilation, and the virtual machine evaluation loop. Option e is false because tokenization precedes parsing.

questions.text: Which of the following built-in Python decorators and language constructs are implemented using the Descriptor Protocol?

options.text: @property (implements __get__, __set__, and __delete__ as a data descriptor)
@classmethod (binds cls as first argument via __get__ as a non-data descriptor)
@staticmethod (returns the raw function without binding self or cls via __get__)
Regular instance methods (binds self via __get__ when accessed through an instance)
Local variables defined inside a function scope

questions.explanation: Properties, classmethods, staticmethods, and standard functions all implement the descriptor protocol via `__get__` (and `__set__` for properties). Local variables are stored on the frame stack, not via descriptors.

questions.text:
Review the following box-joining diagram connecting Python concurrency primitives (Boxes 1-3) with dashes to their execution characteristics:
[Box 1: threading.Thread]        -- (dash) --> [OS threads sharing memory but constrained by the GIL for CPU-bound tasks]
[Box 2: multiprocessing.Process] -- (dash) --> [Independent OS processes with separate memory and isolated GILs]
[Box 3: asyncio.Task]            -- (dash) --> [Single-threaded cooperative multitasking scheduled via an OS I/O event loop]
Which of these concurrency connections are accurate?

options.text: Box 1 accurately describes OS threads constrained by CPython's GIL
Box 2 accurately describes isolated processes with independent GILs
Box 3 accurately describes single-threaded cooperative coroutines on an event loop
Box 3 accurately describes multi-core preemptive CPU scheduling across kernel threads

questions.explanation: Threads share memory but run under the GIL; processes run independent Python interpreters; asyncio runs a single-threaded cooperative event loop without preemptive thread scheduling.
